name: Fret
seoDesc: Fret: a free other calculator that walks you through 28 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary:
The Fret calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports the result immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer.

Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Fret calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fret calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fret calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

1st fret=(1 ÷ 2) × scale length × (2 − (2 ^ 11 ÷ 12))
2nd fret=(1 ÷ 2) × scale length × (2 − (2 ^ 5 ÷ 6))
3rd fret=(1 ÷ 2) × scale length × (2 − (2 ^ 3 ÷ 4))
4th fret=(1 ÷ 2) × scale length × (2 − (2 ^ 2 ÷ 3))
5th fret=(1 ÷ 2) × scale length × (2 − (2 ^ 7 ÷ 12))
Scale length=the square root of (2) × 6th fret + 2 × 6th fret

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Scale length = 30 cm. Working through the relationship above gives 1st fret = 2 mm, 2nd fret = 3 mm, 3rd fret = 5 mm and 4th fret = 6 mm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: 1st fret = 2 mm, 2nd fret = 3 mm, 3rd fret = 5 mm and 4th fret = 6 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Scale length = 30 cm.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fret calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fret calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is a single field. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter scale length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Scale length opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports 1st fret = 2 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fret calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
